results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: Among non-example targets of multi-example sets, yes rate when the target is strictly closer to the first-shown example than to the last-shown one minus yes rate when strictly closer to the last; observed differing from null means presentation order matters (positive = primacy, negative = recency), which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: Among non-example targets of multi-example sets, yes rate when the target is strictly closer to the first-shown example than to the last-shown one minus yes rate when strictly closer to the last; observed differing from null means presentation order matters (positive = primacy, negative = recency), which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = list(sets.unique())
    pad = np.full((len(uniq), 4), -1000, dtype=int)
    n_ex = np.zeros(len(uniq), dtype=int)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        a = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:4]
        pad[i, :len(a)] = a
        n_ex[i] = len(a)
    idx = sets.map({s: i for i, s in enumerate(uniq)}).to_numpy()
    ex = pad[idx]
    k = n_ex[idx]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    f = ex[:, 0]
    l = ex[np.arange(len(t)), np.maximum(k - 1, 0)]
    valid = (k >= 2) & ~is_ex
    dfirst = np.abs(t - f)
    dlast = np.abs(t - l)
    a = valid & (dfirst < dlast)
    b = valid & (dlast < dfirst)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: power2_set_even_generalization
results.description: Yes rate on even, non-power-of-two, non-example targets for sets of two or more examples that are all powers of two; observed above null means people generalize from power-of-two examples to "even numbers" more than the (tempered) size principle allows, below means they lock onto powers of two more tightly.
results.code:
# name: power2_set_even_generalization
# description: Yes rate on even, non-power-of-two, non-example targets for sets of two or more examples that are all powers of two; observed above null means people generalize from power-of-two examples to "even numbers" more than the (tempered) size principle allows, below means they lock onto powers of two more tightly.
def test_statistic(df):
    p2 = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ok = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        a = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = len(a) >= 2 and all(e in p2 for e in a)
    m = sets.map(ok).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    notp2 = ~np.isin(t, list(p2))
    sel = m & (t % 2 == 0) & notp2
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0

results.name: cell_unanimity_rate
results.description: Fraction of (number_set, target) cells answered more than once in which every response is identical; observed above null means people agree more deterministically than the model predicts (its guessing/posterior is too noisy, cell probabilities not extreme enough), below means less.

results.name: single_example_distance_slope
results.description: Least-squares slope of yes (0/1) on |target - example| / 10 for non-example targets of single-example sets; observed more negative than null means people's generalization from one example falls off with numerical distance more steeply than the model's interval/rule mixture predicts, less negative means flatter.
results.code:
# name: single_example_distance_slope
# description: Least-squares slope of yes (0/1) on |target - example| / 10 for non-example targets of single-example sets; observed more negative than null means people's generalization from one example falls off with numerical distance more steeply than the model's interval/rule mixture predicts, less negative means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~sets.str.contains(",", regex=False).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    e = pd.to_numeric(sets.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = single & (t != e)
    if sel.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = np.abs(t[sel] - e[sel]) / 10.0
    y = r[sel]
    vx = np.var(x)
    if vx <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.mean((x - x.mean()) * (y - y.mean())) / vx)

results.name: shared_rule_set_out_of_range_yes
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets outside the [min,max] example range, restricted to multi-example sets whose examples all share a last digit or are all multiples of the same n in 3..12; observed above null means people extend a clear arithmetic rule beyond the example range more than the model (too much interval mass), below means less.
results.code:
# name: shared_rule_set_out_of_range_yes
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets outside the [min,max] example range, restricted to multi-example sets whose examples all share a last digit or are all multiples of the same n in 3..12; observed above null means people extend a clear arithmetic rule beyond the example range more than the model (too much interval mass), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = list(sets.unique())
    info = {}
    for s in uniq:
        a = np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")])
        rule = False
        if len(a) >= 2:
            rule = bool(np.all(a % 10 == a[0] % 10)) or any(np.all(a % n == 0) for n in range(3, 13))
        info[s] = (rule, a.min(), a.max(), s)
    rule = sets.map({s: v[0] for s, v in info.items()}).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    lo = sets.map({s: v[1] for s, v in info.items()}).to_numpy()
    hi = sets.map({s: v[2] for s, v in info.items()}).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = rule & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0

results.name: participant_consensus_agreement_sd
results.description: SD across participants (sessions delimited by trial_index resets to 0) of each participant's mean agreement 1-|r - leave-one-out cell mean| with the others' responses in the same (set, target) cell; observed above null means participants differ in how noisy/rule-consistent they are (individual differences the single-parameter model lacks), below means more homogeneous.
results.code:
# name: participant_consensus_agreement_sd
# description: SD across participants (sessions delimited by trial_index resets to 0) of each participant's mean agreement 1-|r - leave-one-out cell mean| with the others' responses in the same (set, target) cell; observed above null means participants differ in how noisy/rule-consistent they are (individual differences the single-parameter model lacks), below means more homogeneous.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy().astype(int)
    pid = np.cumsum(ti == 0)
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str) + "|" + df["target"].astype(str)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    s = pd.Series(r).groupby(key.to_numpy()).transform("sum").to_numpy()
    n = pd.Series(r).groupby(key.to_numpy()).transform("size").to_numpy()
    ok = n >= 2
    if not ok.any():
        return 0.0
    loo = (s[ok] - r[ok]) / (n[ok] - 1)
    agree = 1 - np.abs(r[ok] - loo)
    per = pd.Series(agree).groupby(pid[ok]).mean()
    if len(per) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(per.std(ddof=1))

results.name: first_presentation_minus_repeat
results.description: Within each participant session (trial_index resets to 0), yes rate on the first trial a given example set appears minus yes rate on later trials with that same set; observed differing from null means generalization shifts with repeated exposure to a set (positive = narrowing, negative = broadening), which the stationary model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: first_presentation_minus_repeat
# description: Within each participant session (trial_index resets to 0), yes rate on the first trial a given example set appears minus yes rate on later trials with that same set; observed differing from null means generalization shifts with repeated exposure to a set (positive = narrowing, negative = broadening), which the stationary model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy().astype(int)
    pid = np.cumsum(ti == 0)
    key = pd.Series(pid.astype(str)) + "|" + pd.Series(df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy())
    order = np.lexsort((ti, pid))
    first = np.zeros(len(ti), dtype=bool)
    first[order] = ~key.iloc[order].duplicated().to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    rep = ~first
    if not first.any() or not rep.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[first].mean() - r[rep].mean())

results.name: opposite_parity_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on targets whose parity differs from all examples, for multi-example sets whose examples are all even or all odd; observed below null means the model's guessing floor over-produces yeses on clearly rule-violating targets, above means it under-produces them.
results.code:
# name: opposite_parity_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on targets whose parity differs from all examples, for multi-example sets whose examples are all even or all odd; observed below null means the model's guessing floor over-produces yeses on clearly rule-violating targets, above means it under-produces them.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    par = {}
    for s in uniq:
        a = np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")])
        if len(a) >= 2 and np.all(a % 2 == a[0] % 2):
            par[s] = float(a[0] % 2)
        else:
            par[s] = -1.0
    p = sets.map(par).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = (p >= 0) & ((t % 2) != p)
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0
